plan.contextChunk: This figure contains four sub-panels (a through d) showing the different matrix representations used to encode a graph for graph neural networks. Panel a) depicts a 6-node undirected graph with nodes labeled 1 through 6, connected by edges whose identities are marked by the pair of endpoint node labels (e.g., ‘1\3’, ‘1\4’, ‘2\3’, ‘3\4’, ‘3\6’, ‘4\5’, ‘5\6’). Panel b) shows the adjacency matrix A (N × N), a square binary matrix encoding which pairs of nodes are connected by edges. Panel c) shows the node feature matrix X (D × N), in which each column stores the D-dimensional feature vector associated with one of the N nodes. Panel d) shows the edge feature matrix E (Dᴷ × E), in which each column stores the Dᴷ-dimensional feature vector associated with one of the E edges, with edges ordered to match the labeled pairs in panel a). Labels for each matrix include its name, symbol, and dimensions. This figure introduces the three standard data structures—adjacency matrix, node feature matrix, and edge feature matrix—that together fully represent a graph with node and edge attributes in a deep learning context.

interactionPlan.concept: A graph with attributes is fully encoded for deep learning by three matrices: the adjacency matrix A (who connects to whom), the node data matrix X (a feature column per node), and the edge data matrix E (a feature column per edge).
elements: Panel label 'a)' top-left of the graph panel

Undirected graph with six circular nodes outlined in dark rust-brown, labeled 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, laid out as in the figure: node 2 far left-upper, node 1 upper-center, node 4 upper-right, node 5 right, node 3 left-center (hub), node 6 bottom-center
Per-node feature vector glyphs: a vertical stack of 5 small rounded squares in orange/rust shades placed beside each node
Per-edge feature vector glyphs: a vertical stack of 4 small rounded squares in teal shades placed beside the midpoint of each edge
Panel label 'b)' with caption 'Adjacency matrix, A' and dimension text 'N × N' in slate blue
6×6 grid of rounded square cells with column headers 1–6 above and row headers 1–6 at left; filled slate-blue cells at the symmetric positions of the seven edges, white cells elsewhere, zero diagonal
Panel label 'c)' with caption 'Node data, X' and dimension text 'D × N' in rust-brown
5-row × 6-column grid of rounded squares in varied orange/rust shades, with column headers 1–6 matching node indices
Panel label 'd)' with caption 'Edge data, E' and dimension text 'D_E × E' in teal
4-row × 7-column grid of rounded squares in varied teal shades, with two-line column headers giving each edge's endpoint pair (1/3, 1/4, 2/3, 3/4, 3/6, 4/5, 5/6)
Highlight ring / outline styling reserved for selected node, selected edge, and the corresponding highlighted matrix row, column, and cell

interactions.teaches: That a single node is simultaneously a row AND a column of A (symmetry of an undirected graph) and exactly one column of the node data matrix X.
That an edge is one column of E and, at the same time, the two mirrored non-zero entries (i,j) and (j,i) of A — connectivity and edge attributes live in different structures.
What any individual matrix cell means — e.g. 'A[3,4] = 1: nodes 3 and 4 are connected' or 'X[2,5]: feature 2 of node 5' — without cluttering the figure with permanent labels.

demo_steps.title: The graph itself
demo_steps.narration: Six nodes joined by seven undirected edges. Each node carries a D-dimensional feature vector (orange stack) and each edge a D_E-dimensional vector (teal stack) — the picture holds all the information, but a network cannot consume a picture.

demo_steps.title: Connectivity becomes a matrix
demo_steps.narration: The adjacency matrix A puts a 1 wherever two nodes share an edge. It is N × N, symmetric because edges are undirected, and zero on the diagonal because no node links to itself.

demo_steps.title: Click a node: a row, a column, a feature vector
demo_steps.narration: Click node 3 (the hub). Its row and its column in A light up, showing four neighbours mirrored across the diagonal, and column 3 of X lights up — the one place its attributes live.

demo_steps.title: Node attributes live in X
demo_steps.narration: X is D × N: one column per node, one row per feature channel. Node ordering here is arbitrary but must match the ordering used by A.

demo_steps.title: Click an edge: one column of E, two cells of A
demo_steps.narration: Click the edge 3–4. A single column of E holds its attributes, while the same edge appears twice in A, at (3,4) and (4,3). E has E columns — seven, not thirty-six — so edge features are stored sparsely.

demo_steps.title: Three matrices, one graph
demo_steps.narration: Together A, X and E reconstruct the drawing exactly: structure, node attributes, edge attributes. This triple is the standard input to a graph neural network.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A graph is not one array but three: adjacency stores structure, X stores what each node is, E stores what each edge is — and clicking any node or edge shows the same object appearing once in the picture and once (or twice, by symmetry) in each matrix.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Four-panel layout: panel a) occupies the left half, panels b) center-right, c) top-right, d) bottom-right. Palette: nodes as white circles with dark rust-brown outlines and numerals; edges as medium slate-blue lines about 2px; node feature squares in oranges/rusts; edge feature squares in teals; adjacency cells filled slate-blue for 1 and white with grey outline for 0. All matrix cells are small rounded squares with visible gaps. Column/row index labels in dark grey above and left of the adjacency grid; edge-data columns get two stacked digits naming the endpoint pair. Captions sit to the left of each matrix in the matrix's own colour, with name in bold-ish text, symbol in bold math, and dimensions in italic math below. Edge set: 1-3, 1-4, 2-3, 3-4, 3-6, 4-5, 5-6; node 3 is the high-degree hub in the left-center. Highlighting should use a saturated outline plus slight dimming of unselected elements, applied consistently across graph and matrices so the correspondence is unmistakable.

discrepancies: Panel composition differs: the source is a wide single-row arrangement (large graph on the left, b) in the middle, c) above d) on the right), while the generated figure uses a 2×2 quadrant grid, which shrinks panel a) considerably and shifts c) under the graph.

Because panel a) is compressed into one quadrant, the node circles, node numerals and the orange/teal feature stacks render much smaller than in the source, and several stacks sit very close to (or slightly overlap) edge lines around nodes 1, 3 and 6.

Matrix titles ('Adjacency matrix, A', 'Node data, X', 'Edge data, E') are proportionally smaller than in the source, where they are the dominant typographic element; the a)/b)/c)/d) panel letters are also less prominent.

Minor color/value drift in the data stacks and in the X/E matrices — the source uses a few very dark rust and deep teal tiles that give more contrast; generated palettes are somewhat flatter (though the hue families are right).

Node feature stacks in the source are placed consistently beside each node with clear whitespace; in the generated version a couple of stacks (node 3's and edge 2–3's) crowd each other in the left cluster.
evaluation.notes: Structurally faithful and conceptually excellent (correct 6-node/7-edge graph, correct symmetric adjacency pattern, correct D×N and D_E×E matrices, strong cross-panel highlighting and a well-written 6-step demo), but the 2×2 quadrant layout departs from the source's wide composition and shrinks panel a) so its numerals and feature stacks become cramped and small.
action_items: Rework the layout to match the source: give panel a) a tall left column (~55% width), place b) centre, and stack c) above d) on the right, so the graph is drawn at a comparable scale to the source.
Increase font sizes / stroke weights in panel a) (node numerals, panel letters) and enlarge the matrix titles so they read as the dominant labels as in the source.
Nudge the orange/teal feature stacks away from edge lines and from each other in the crowded left cluster (nodes 2/3 and edges 1–3, 2–3) to eliminate overlap.
Deepen the darkest tiles in the orange and teal palettes to restore the source's tonal contrast within each stack and within X/E.

feedback.rationale: Concept, panels, and interactions are correct; the remaining issues are layout proportions, font/stroke sizing, stack spacing, and palette contrast, which are concrete rendering fixes.

demo_steps.title: Node attributes live in X
demo_steps.narration: X is D × N: one column per node, one row per feature channel. Node ordering here is arbitrary but must match the ordering used by A.

demo_steps.title: Click an edge: one column of E, two cells of A
demo_steps.narration: Click the edge 3–4. A single column of E holds its attributes, while the same edge appears twice in A, at (3,4) and (4,3). E has E columns — seven, not thirty-six — so edge features are stored sparsely.

demo_steps.title: Three matrices, one graph
demo_steps.narration: Together A, X and E reconstruct the drawing exactly: structure, node attributes, edge attributes. This triple is the standard input to a graph neural network.

plan.keyInsight: A graph is not one array but three: adjacency stores structure, X stores what each node is, E stores what each edge is — and clicking any node or edge shows the same object appearing once in the picture and once (or twice, by symmetry) in each matrix.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Four-panel layout: panel a) occupies the left half, panels b) center-right, c) top-right, d) bottom-right. Palette: nodes as white circles with dark rust-brown outlines and numerals; edges as medium slate-blue lines about 2px; node feature squares in oranges/rusts; edge feature squares in teals; adjacency cells filled slate-blue for 1 and white with grey outline for 0. All matrix cells are small rounded squares with visible gaps. Column/row index labels in dark grey above and left of the adjacency grid; edge-data columns get two stacked digits naming the endpoint pair. Captions sit to the left of each matrix in the matrix's own colour, with name in bold-ish text, symbol in bold math, and dimensions in italic math below. Edge set: 1-3, 1-4, 2-3, 3-4, 3-6, 4-5, 5-6; node 3 is the high-degree hub in the left-center. Highlighting should use a saturated outline plus slight dimming of unselected elements, applied consistently across graph and matrices so the correspondence is unmistakable.

discrepancies: In panel a) several orange/teal feature stacks sit directly on top of the edge lines and node circles (notably around node 3, node 6 and the 3–6 edge), whereas in the source every stack is cleanly offset into empty space beside its node/edge — the generated graph panel reads as cluttered.

Overall scale: the 1660×620 viewbox is squeezed into the available inline width, so matrix row/column index digits (26px) and node numbers (28px) render at roughly 9–10 px and are noticeably harder to read than in the source, where the indices are prominent.

Panel proportions differ from the source: the graph panel is comparatively wide/compressed and the node circles are small relative to the stacks, so node labels feel cramped compared with the generously spaced source layout.

Node-feature stacks in the generated graph are positioned at fixed offsets that do not reproduce the source's placement pattern (e.g. node 2's stack appears to the right and partly overlapping the circle rather than clearly to its right side), a minor compositional drift.

Generated figure adds a persistent 'a) b) c) d)' plus a side panel narration/status text; this is fine as UI, but the highlight rings (orange) are an added mark type not present in the static source (acceptable as interaction affordance, only visible when selected).
evaluation.notes: Faithful four-panel reproduction with correct graph topology, correctly derived symmetric adjacency matrix, correct X (5×6) and E (4×7) with matching edge-endpoint double headers, plus genuinely useful cross-panel highlighting, dropdowns and a 6-step guided demo; main weaknesses are feature stacks overlapping edges/nodes in panel a) and index/label text rendering uncomfortably small at inline scale.

feedback.rationale: Concept, panels, and interactions are correct; remaining issues are implementation details (stack overlap in panel a and undersized index/node text at inline scale) best fixed by adjusting layout and font sizing in the generator.
